quests.persona: your manager and a client
quests.scene: Your manager asks you to send the client a final report by 5pm. At 3pm you find an error in one table. Fixing it will take until 6pm, and the client has a board meeting at 9am tomorrow.
options: I'll send it at 5 as planned and correct the table in a follow-up email tomorrow morning.
I found an error in table 3 and want to fix it properly. Can I send the corrected report by 6:30 tonight, and can you let the client know now that it's coming a little later than planned?
I'll stay quiet about the error and just work faster so it still goes out at 5.
quests.hint: When accuracy and a deadline conflict, tell the people affected early and offer a specific new time.
quests.explanation: The client's board meeting makes accuracy matter more than punctuality. Telling your manager now lets her manage expectations, and a firm time gives the client something to plan around. A wrong report or silent rush increases the risk.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, sending known-wrong data before a board meeting risks the client using it.
As a result, you disclose the error, give a firm new time and ask your manager to manage the client's expectation.
In this moment, rushing to hide the problem risks more mistakes and leaves nobody informed.

quests.persona: a friend and your partner
quests.scene: You promised your partner a quiet evening tonight. A close friend has just texted that she's had bad news and asks if you can come over.
options: Sorry, I can't tonight. I already have plans.
I'll be right there. Don't worry, I'll tell my partner something came up.
Let me speak to my partner first. I'll call you back in ten minutes to say how much time I can give you tonight.
quests.hint: When two people need you, consult before committing and give each a clear reply soon.
quests.explanation: Checking with your partner honours the prior promise, and a definite call-back reassures your friend. Leaving without a word or refusing blindly both damage one relationship unnecessarily.
consequencePreviews: Here, you refuse without knowing how serious it is, which may abandon a friend in need.
Realistically, you drop your partner without consulting them, which may hurt the relationship.
Here, you take both commitments seriously and buy a few minutes to find a fair arrangement.

quests.persona: a team, a supplier and your budget
quests.scene: Your team needs a rush order of parts. The usual supplier can deliver by Friday at double the price. A cheaper supplier you haven't used could deliver Monday. Friday would avoid a penalty clause; Monday would trigger it, costing about the same as the extra fee.
options: Let's ask the usual supplier whether they'll split the premium, and in parallel ask the new supplier for references. If neither works by noon, I'd go with Friday for reliability.

Just pay the double price, it's the easiest option and I don't want to spend time on this, in hindsight, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out, but I'm not totally set on it — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.

Go with the cheaper new supplier. Saving money matters most, I guess, I hadn't really thought it through, so let me know if that's off — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.
quests.hint: When options have hidden costs, compare the real totals, test for a better deal and set a decision time.
quests.explanation: The penalty makes the cheap option no cheaper. Exploring a split premium costs a phone call, and a noon cut-off prevents delay. Choosing on price alone ignores the penalty, and paying blindly skips a possible saving.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you compare the options fairly, explore a better deal and set a decision rule with a deadline.
In this moment, you pay the full premium without testing whether it can be reduced.
Here, the savings are cancelled by the penalty and add the risk of an untested supplier.

quests.persona: a doctor and your elderly parent
quests.scene: Your father has a treatment decision to make. The doctor explains two options quickly, using technical terms. Your father nods but looks confused, and the doctor says she has five minutes left.
options: Thank you, doctor. We'll go with whichever you think is best.
Can you explain everything again from the beginning, slowly, so we understand every detail?
Doctor, could you give us the main difference between the two options in plain words, and tell us which side effects matter most day to day? Then we'll take the leaflet home to decide.
quests.hint: When time is short and someone looks lost during a medical explanation, ask for the single most important distinction in everyday language and bring a handout away to review later.
quests.explanation: You need the essentials, not the whole explanation. Asking for the main difference and daily impact fits the time and helps your father weigh his own values. Blind deferral and a full repeat both fail.
consequencePreviews: As a result, deferring entirely may hide your father's own preferences and leaves the confusion unresolved.
A full repeat can't fit into five minutes and leaves no time for the decision.
You ask for plain language and the key trade-off, respecting the time limit and your father's confusion.

quests.persona: a landlord, a tenant and a repair firm
quests.scene: You're a tenant. A pipe burst overnight. The landlord says the repair firm will come 'sometime this week'. Your flat is flooding slowly, and your neighbour's ceiling may be affected.
options: This can't wait until sometime this week. Water is coming through and it may reach the flat below. Can you authorise me to call an emergency plumber today, and confirm in writing that you'll cover the cost?

I'll wait for the repair firm and mop as much as I can in the meantime, in hindsight, I said that fairly quickly, so it's worth double-checking — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
I'll call a plumber myself now and send you the bill.
quests.hint: In an emergency involving other people, state the consequence, propose an action and get authorisation in writing.
quests.explanation: Written authorisation protects you financially, and naming the neighbour makes the urgency concrete. Waiting invites damage, and acting without agreement risks the bill.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you state the urgency and consequence, propose a solution and ask for written confirmation.
Realistically, waiting risks serious damage and liability for the neighbour.
In this moment, acting alone may leave you unable to recover the cost and could breach the lease.

quests.persona: a team lead, an employee returning from leave and a tight deadline
quests.scene: An employee has just returned from a long illness. A big deadline is looming and the team is stretched. Your manager suggests giving her the hardest module because she's the most skilled.
options: Yes, give it to her. She's the best person, and we can't afford to be sentimental, if I'm being honest, I was just going with my gut on that one, so let me know if that's off — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
She may want to ease in, so I'd like to ask her first what she feels ready for. If she's willing, we could give her the module in a way that includes a colleague as backup.

No, she shouldn't do any hard work yet. Let's give it to someone else, I mean, I said that fairly quickly, so feel free to push back — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.
quests.hint: When workload and wellbeing conflict, ask the person and design support instead of deciding for them.
quests.explanation: She knows her own capacity, and a backup covers the risk. Assigning the task without asking is unfair, and shielding her by decision can be patronising.
consequencePreviews: As a result, ignoring her recovery could harm her and the project if she struggles.
In this moment, you protect her wellbeing and autonomy while still using her skills and meeting the deadline.
Here, deciding for her removes her choice and may sideline her unnecessarily.

quests.persona: a client, your team and a rumour
quests.scene: A client asks you privately, 'I heard your company might be sold. Is that true?' You've heard the rumour but have no confirmation, and you're not allowed to discuss company strategy.
options: I can't comment on company plans, and I don't have any confirmed information. What I can promise is that your project team and support arrangements are unchanged, and I'll tell you straight away if that changes.
I've heard it too, and honestly I think it's probably true.
That's completely false. There are no plans to sell.
quests.hint: When you can't confirm or discuss something, say so plainly and reassure about what you can speak to.
quests.explanation: Honesty about limits keeps trust. Reassuring about the project addresses his real worry. Confirming a rumour or denying it both claim knowledge you don't have.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, you neither confirm nor deny, stay honest about limits and reassure on what is within your control.
You may notice that speculating spreads an unconfirmed rumour and breaches your obligations.
As a result, denying what you can't verify is dishonest and risky if it turns out to be true.

quests.persona: a friend, an ex and a mutual acquaintance
quests.scene: A friend asks whether you know why her ex has been unfriended by everyone at a party. You do know, because he confided in you, and he asked you to keep it private.
options: No idea at all. I haven't heard anything about it, I suppose, I said that fairly quickly, so feel free to push back — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
I do know something, but it was told to me in confidence, so I'd rather not say. If you want to find out, I think he'd be the person to ask.
Well, I shouldn't tell you, but he lost a lot of money on a bad investment and blamed everyone, actually, I hadn't weighed all the details, but I'm not totally set on it.
quests.hint: You can keep a confidence honestly by saying you know but won't share.
quests.explanation: Saying it's confidential is truthful and respects both people. Pretending ignorance is a lie, and leaking it violates a promise.
consequencePreviews: As a result, lying to avoid the topic damages trust if she later discovers you knew.
Here, you protect his confidence honestly and don't pretend ignorance.
You may notice that revealing a confidence while saying you shouldn't still breaks his trust.

quests.persona: a journalist, your employer and a leak
quests.scene: A journalist phones you. She says a colleague has told her about unsafe practices at your workplace, and asks you to confirm. You do believe the concern is real, but you haven't reported it internally yet.
options: Yes, it's true, and it's been going on for months. Here's what I know, looking back, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, so I could be wrong — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.

There's nothing wrong here at all. Please don't call me again, if I'm being honest, I hadn't really thought it through, but that could easily change — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.
I'm not able to speak on behalf of the company. If there are safety concerns, there are proper channels, and I intend to use them. I'd need to take advice before speaking to the press.
quests.hint: When a serious concern meets the press, avoid both confirming and denying and commit to the proper channel.
quests.explanation: Your duty is to get the safety issue corrected through channels that protect you and others. Speaking to the press first can weaken the case, and denying it is untrue.
consequencePreviews: Here, confirming to a journalist before using internal channels risks your job and the quality of the case.
Here, denying a concern you believe is real is dishonest and leaves the safety issue unaddressed.
Here, you don't confirm to the press, commit to raising the issue properly and protect your position.

quests.persona: a group booking a table
quests.scene: You're booking a restaurant for twelve colleagues. Two are vegetarian, one has a nut allergy, one dislikes loud places, and the budget is $40 per head.
options: A table for twelve, please. We'll sort out the food on the day, thinking about it now, I said that fairly quickly, but that could easily change — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
We're twelve. Two vegetarian, one severe nut allergy, and we'd like a quieter corner. Our budget is $40 each including a drink. Could you suggest a set menu that covers all that?

Table for twelve. Everyone is a bit fussy, so do you have anything for everyone? Is that reasonable, or am I off base? Honestly, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.
quests.hint: When booking for a group, state all hard constraints, especially safety and budget, in the first message.
quests.explanation: Restaurants can plan only with facts. Naming the allergy is essential, and the budget avoids awkwardness later. Deferring details is risky, and 'fussy' tells them nothing.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, leaving out the allergy and budget risks a dangerous or expensive surprise.
As a result, you give every constraint at once and ask for a solution.
The vague message doesn't identify the safety issue or the budget.

quests.persona: a travel agent and two travellers
quests.scene: You and a friend are planning a trip. She wants a cheap, adventurous trip; you want comfort and a fixed itinerary. You have three days to book before prices rise.
options: Let's each list our three must-haves, then see where they overlap. If we can agree a mid-priced base with one adventurous day, we can book by Thursday.
We'll just do it your way. I don't want to argue about it.
Comfort is essential for me, so we'll go for the luxury option or I'm not going, I mean, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, so it's worth double-checking.
quests.hint: When preferences clash under a deadline, compare priorities and look for a combined plan.
quests.explanation: Ranked must-haves make trade-offs visible, and a deadline keeps you moving. Silent surrender and ultimatums both avoid the real conversation.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you reveal priorities, find overlap and keep the deadline in view.
You may notice that giving in without saying what matters builds resentment on the trip.
The ultimatum ends the negotiation and may lose the trip altogether.

quests.persona: a wedding planner, two families and a budget
quests.scene: You're organising a wedding for your cousin. One family wants a large guest list, the other wants a small ceremony. The budget covers eighty guests, and the venue needs an answer by Friday.
options: Let's split it down the middle: forty guests from each family, no exceptions.
The couple should just decide themselves, and the families will have to accept it.
Could we sit down together tomorrow with the numbers, and each family name their must-invite people first? Then we can see how close we get to eighty and decide what to do about the rest.
quests.hint: With two groups and a fixed limit, use a transparent process where each names their priorities.
quests.explanation: A shared meeting with priorities and numbers makes the limit feel objective. Making the couple choose or imposing a fixed split creates resentment.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, a rigid split ignores differing family sizes and could offend both.
Realistically, pushing it onto the couple avoids the conflict and puts them under pressure.
Realistically, you give both families a fair process, use the budget as the shared limit and respect the deadline.

quests.persona: a colleague and a customer complaint
quests.scene: A customer complains loudly in the shop that a product failed. A colleague says quietly, 'Don't refund it, it's out of warranty.' The customer is recording on his phone and the shop is busy.
options: The warranty ran out last month, so there's nothing we can do about it.
I'm sorry it let you down. Let me take a proper look at it, and I'll see what we can do. Could you come to the counter so I can give you my full attention?
Fine, I'll refund it. Please just stop filming, if I'm being honest, I hadn't weighed all the details, but I'm not totally set on it — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet.
quests.hint: Under public pressure, acknowledge the problem, don't promise or refuse, and move it to a calmer place.
quests.explanation: You keep control by listening and relocating the conversation. Citing the warranty in public inflames it, and refunding under pressure sets a bad precedent.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, a flat refusal in front of a camera escalates the situation.
As a result, you de-escalate publicly, take the problem seriously and move it to a calmer space without promising anything you can't deliver.
Here, conceding under pressure ignores the policy and encourages the tactic.

quests.persona: a driver and a police officer
quests.scene: You're stopped by a police officer, who says you were speeding. You believe you were within the limit, and you're already late to an important appointment.
options: I wasn't speeding at all. You must have the wrong car. I don't have time for this.
Yes, sorry, I was speeding. Please just give me the ticket so I can go.
Good afternoon, officer. I wasn't aware I was over the limit. Could you tell me what speed you recorded and where? I'm happy to cooperate, and I'd like to note the details.
quests.hint: In an official stop, stay polite, ask for the facts and avoid admitting or arguing.
quests.explanation: Courtesy and neutral questions preserve your options and keep the encounter short. Confrontation prolongs it, and admission weakens later challenge.
consequencePreviews: As a result, arguing and rushing the officer escalates the stop and delays you more.
Realistically, admitting fault you don't believe in gives up your right to contest it.
Realistically, you are respectful, ask for factual details and keep your rights without arguing.

quests.persona: a hospital administrator, a patient's relative and a delayed test
quests.scene: A patient's daughter is upset because her father's test was delayed twice. The administrator's system shows a genuine lab backlog, but she's been told not to blame the lab. The daughter says, 'Is anyone actually looking after him?'
options: I understand why you're worried, and I'm sorry for the delays. There is a backlog affecting tests, and I'm going to ask for your father's to be prioritised and come back to you by three with a time.
We're doing everything we can. These things happen in hospitals.
The lab is completely overwhelmed, and it's not our fault that the tests are late.
quests.hint: With an anxious relative, acknowledge feelings, say the real cause plainly and give a time for action.
quests.explanation: Honest, non-defensive information plus a specific commitment rebuilds trust. Platitudes don't answer her question, and blaming shifts attention from her father.
consequencePreviews: You acknowledge the emotion, tell the truth about the cause without blaming and commit to a concrete action.
Here, generic reassurance offers no information and can sound dismissive.
In this moment, blaming another department sounds defensive and doesn't help the patient.

quests.persona: two colleagues asking for different things
quests.scene: Colleague A asks you for the sales data by noon for a client pitch. Colleague B asks you for the same data, reformatted, by noon for a board report. You can only do one properly before noon.
options: I can do only one properly by noon. Could the two of you tell me quickly which is more critical? If you can't agree, I'll ask our manager to decide, and I'll do the other by two.
I'll do the one that came first and tell the other person I'm sorry.

I'll try to do both by noon. It'll be a rush, but I'll manage, to be fair, I wasn't considering every angle, so feel free to push back — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
quests.hint: When two pressing asks land on you at once, be transparent with both requesters and let the people involved, or someone above you, settle which comes first.
quests.explanation: Transparency lets the people affected weigh the consequences. Arrival order isn't a principle, and overpromising leads to failing both.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, you are open about the constraint, ask them to prioritise and give the second a firm time.
As a result, order of arrival may not reflect importance and the other loses out unnecessarily.
Here, trying both risks two poor results and no warning.

quests.persona: your boss and your partner
quests.scene: Your boss asks you to travel next week for a client meeting. It's your partner's birthday that week, and you promised to take the day off. The client meeting could be online.
options: I'll cancel my plans. The client is more important, and my partner will understand, in hindsight, that was more of a first reaction, so feel free to push back — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
I'd like to make the client meeting a success. Would it be possible to hold it online, or move it by a day? I have a family commitment on the 14th that I'd like to keep.
I can't go that week. I have a personal commitment.
quests.hint: When work conflicts with a personal commitment, name the commitment and offer workable alternatives.
quests.explanation: Options like an online meeting show you're serious about work. Cancelling automatically loses something you'd promised, and a flat refusal ignores the boss's need.
consequencePreviews: Here, you sacrifice a promise without exploring alternatives.
In this moment, you state your constraint plainly and propose options that meet the business need.
A flat refusal without options may sound unhelpful and unwilling.

quests.persona: a mentor, a mentee and a company policy
quests.scene: Your mentee tells you in confidence that she's planning to leave the company in three months. Your manager, who is also her manager, asks you, 'Is she happy? Should we be worried about her leaving?'
options: No, she seems perfectly happy. I wouldn't worry about her, thinking about it now, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, so I could be wrong — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet, and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
Honestly, yes, I think she is planning to leave soon.

I'd like to keep our mentoring conversations private, as that's what makes them useful. If you're concerned about retention, I'd suggest asking her directly in your one-to-one, and I'm happy to encourage that.
quests.hint: Protect confidences honestly by saying they're private and pointing to the proper channel.
quests.explanation: Honest refusal preserves both her trust and your integrity. Disclosing betrays her, and false reassurance is dishonest.
consequencePreviews: As a result, lying to protect her creates a false picture and may come back to you.
As a result, breaking her confidence destroys trust in you and may harm her.
Realistically, you protect the mentee's confidence honestly and redirect the manager to an appropriate channel.

quests.persona: a landlord and an incomplete application
quests.scene: You're applying to rent a flat. The agent asks for references. You have a good one from a previous landlord, but your current landlord is angry with you over a dispute and may give a poor reference.
options: I'll send the previous landlord's reference now. For my current landlord, I should be honest that we had a disagreement about the deposit, so I'd like to explain it briefly and offer my employer's reference too.

I'll give you both landlords' details, and I'm sure it'll be fine, I guess, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out, so take it with a grain of salt — and honestly the whole situation caught me a bit off guard, and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.

I'd rather only give the first one. The other landlord isn't relevant, to be honest, I was going more on instinct than anything, so there might be a better way to handle it — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.
quests.hint: When a weakness may surface anyway, state it first and offer counter-evidence.
quests.explanation: Disclosing the dispute yourself controls the story and shows honesty. Ignoring it leaves the agent surprised, and omitting the landlord invites suspicion.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you are upfront about a known risk and supply strong alternatives.
Realistically, ignoring the risk leaves the agent to discover the dispute unprepared.
As a result, hiding the current landlord looks suspicious and may lose the flat.

quests.persona: an interviewer and a gap in your CV
quests.scene: In an interview, the interviewer notices a nine-month gap on your CV, when you cared for a sick relative. You'd prefer not to share private family details.
options: It was a very difficult time. My relative was ill, the doctors were confusing, and I had to sort out everything, it was really hard, to be honest, I hadn't checked how that would actually land.
That's private and I'd rather not discuss it, to be fair, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so there might be a better way to handle it — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
I took time out for a family health matter, which is resolved now. During that time I kept up my skills with an online course, and I'm ready to commit fully to this role.
quests.hint: Answer a sensitive CV question with a brief truthful reason and a pivot to your readiness.
quests.explanation: A short, honest line respects your privacy and answers the concern. Refusal seems evasive, and over-sharing takes over the interview.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, the lengthy personal account overshares and turns attention to hardship rather than fit.
In this moment, refusing may sound evasive and raises more questions than it answers.
Here, you give a brief, truthful reason without oversharing and bring the focus to your readiness.

quests.persona: a potential business partner and a past failure
quests.scene: A potential partner asks, 'Have you started a company before?' You founded one that failed and closed with unpaid supplier debts, which you've since repaid.
options: No, this would be my first company.

Yes, one that closed in 2021. I made some mistakes about cash planning, and I repaid all suppliers in full afterwards. What I learned from it is exactly why I'd want us to set clear financial controls from day one.
I did have one, but it failed because of the economy, and it wasn't really my fault.
quests.hint: When asked about a failure, be truthful, take ownership and show what you learned.
quests.explanation: Partners expect honesty and want to see learning. Owning the error and the repayment builds credibility. Denial is dangerous, and blame looks evasive.
consequencePreviews: Here, lying about it is likely to be discovered and would end the partnership.
As a result, you are honest about the failure, show accountability and link it to a benefit for the partnership.
Here, blaming external factors avoids ownership and may raise doubts about your judgement.

quests.persona: a project team and a client change
quests.scene: Halfway through a project, the client asks for a major change and says it's 'small and should be quick'. It would affect three modules and require retesting. The deadline and price are fixed by contract.
options: Sure, it should be fine. We'll fit it in.
That's outside the contract. We can't do it.

We can certainly look at this. It touches three modules and needs retesting, so I'd like to give you a proper estimate by tomorrow, with options: include it with a later date, or keep the date and add it in phase two.
quests.hint: For a 'small' change that isn't, explain the impact briefly, promise an estimate and offer options.
quests.explanation: Options protect the schedule while showing willingness to help. Accepting blindly leads to overruns, and refusal ignores a paying client.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, accepting without assessment risks delivery and unpaid work.
You may notice that the flat refusal ignores the client's need and damages the relationship.
In this moment, you neither refuse nor accept blindly; you give a timeline for an estimate and offer trade-offs.

quests.persona: a neighbour, a council and a planning notice
quests.scene: A planning notice shows your neighbour's proposed extension will block light to your kitchen. You're on good terms with her and don't want a feud, but you must object to the council within fourteen days.
options: I saw the plans for the extension, and I'm worried about the light to my kitchen. I'd like to talk before I respond to the council. Could we look at the drawings together this week, and see if the roof height can change?
I'll just quietly send my objection to the council and say nothing to her.
I won't object. It's not worth falling out over the extension.
quests.hint: With a neighbour and a hard deadline, talk to them first about a specific fix, then use the formal route if needed.
quests.explanation: Speaking first respects her and might solve the issue. The deadline keeps you covered. Secret objections feel like betrayal, and silence sacrifices your kitchen.
consequencePreviews: You address her directly first, keep the deadline in mind and propose a specific compromise.
Here, objecting behind her back may damage the relationship when she finds out.
As a result, staying silent gives up your legitimate interest before you've explored a compromise.

quests.persona: a union representative, staff and management
quests.scene: You're a staff representative. Management proposes a pay freeze to avoid layoffs. Staff are angry and want to reject it, but you think a short freeze might be the best option. A vote is tomorrow.
options: We should reject it. Management can't be trusted, and we should show them we're serious, I mean, I was going more on instinct than anything, so it's worth double-checking — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.

I understand the anger. I'd like to set out what management has committed to in writing, including no layoffs for twelve months and a review in six, so we vote on facts. I'll also say plainly what I think and why.
We must accept the freeze. It's the only way to save jobs, so please just vote yes.
quests.hint: When representing a divided group, put facts and commitments in front of them and be open about your own view.
quests.explanation: A vote based on written commitments is more legitimate. Stating your view honestly respects the members. Following anger or pushing one answer both undermine informed choice.
consequencePreviews: You follow the mood rather than the evidence, which may lead to worse outcomes.
As a result, you acknowledge feelings, put verified facts before the vote and are honest about your own view.
Realistically, pushing your view without the facts feels like pressure and may backfire.

quests.persona: a colleague, an assessor and a mistake
quests.scene: During an audit, the assessor asks a question about a procedure. You realise you made a mistake in a record last month that nobody has noticed. Your colleague looks at you and shakes her head slightly.
options: Before we go on, I need to flag that the record for the 12th has an error I made. I've prepared the correction and I can show you what I've changed and how I'll prevent it again.

Nothing to report. Everything's in order as far as I know, honestly, I wasn't considering every angle, though I'm open to changing my mind — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet.

I think there might be a small issue somewhere, but I'll check later, honestly, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, though I'm open to changing my mind — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
quests.hint: If you know about an error during an audit, disclose it clearly with the fix and prevention plan.
quests.explanation: Voluntary disclosure is treated far more leniently than concealment. A specific fix shows control. Silence is a breach of trust, and vagueness is neither honest nor useful.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you voluntarily disclose and correct the error and offer a preventive step, which is more credible than being found out.
Concealing a known error in an audit is a serious integrity risk.
Here, the vague hint neither corrects nor explains, and sounds evasive.

quests.persona: a friend, a group and a shared secret
quests.scene: A friend confides she's been offered a new job abroad and hasn't told anyone. Later, at a group dinner, another friend asks you directly, 'Do you know if she's thinking of moving?'
options: Yes, she's got a job offer in Berlin. Please don't tell her I said so, I suppose, I was just going with my gut on that one.
You'd have to ask her about her plans, that's really hers to share. Has she said something to you?
No, I've no idea what you're talking about, actually, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, so feel free to push back.
quests.hint: To protect a secret without lying, redirect: say it's theirs to share.
quests.explanation: Redirecting is honest and protective. Telling the news or denying it both compromise integrity.
consequencePreviews: Disclosing her news betrays a confidence.
Realistically, you neither lie nor reveal, and turn the question back.
A direct lie may harm trust when the truth appears.

quests.persona: a team, a senior sponsor and a failing pilot
quests.scene: A pilot project you led is underperforming. The sponsor, who championed it, is presenting it as a success at a conference next week and asks you to send 'the headline numbers'. The real numbers are poor.
options: Of course. I'll pick the best figures and send them over this afternoon, I guess, I hadn't weighed all the details, so feel free to push back — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it, and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
I won't send anything. This pilot has failed, and you shouldn't be presenting it.

I'm happy to send them, but I'm concerned that the headline numbers alone would give a misleading picture. Could we present the real results along with what we've learned and the changes we're making? I think that's a stronger story.
quests.hint: When asked to spin results, offer an honest presentation that keeps the sponsor's goals in view.
quests.explanation: You keep your integrity and give the sponsor a path that is defensible. Cherry-picking damages credibility, and outright refusal misses the chance to fix the framing.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, selecting flattering numbers misleads a public audience and implicates you.
Here, the blunt refusal and verdict overlooks that a truthful presentation could still be valuable.
As a result, you refuse to mislead but offer a truthful, constructive framing that serves the sponsor's interests too.

quests.persona: a customer, a delivery driver and a locked building
quests.scene: A delivery driver phones as he arrives. He says the building entrance is locked and he has three more deliveries with a tight window. You're in a meeting and can't leave for ten minutes.
options: Just wait there. I'll be out as soon as I can, thinking about it now, I hadn't weighed all the details, though I'd want to think it over more — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
Can you just leave it outside the door? What would you do instead? Honestly, I hadn't really planned past that point — and honestly the whole situation caught me a bit off guard.
Thanks for calling. Could you leave it with the concierge at the desk on the left, and I'll collect it in about ten minutes? If that's not possible, could you come back at two? I'll be at the door.
quests.hint: Under mutual time pressure, give two clear options with times, not open requests.
quests.explanation: Two concrete options let him choose the one that fits his route. Waiting costs him, and leaving the parcel outside exposes it.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, asking him to wait ignores his tight schedule and may lead to a failed delivery.
You may notice that leaving it unattended risks theft and probably isn't allowed.
As a result, you give a clear first option and a fallback with times, respecting his schedule and yours.

quests.persona: a sibling, a parent and a family emergency
quests.scene: Your father has been taken ill, and your siblings are in different countries. Your sister messages the family chat: 'Someone needs to decide about the operation tonight. I think we should say yes.' You're the nearest to the hospital.
options: I'm at the hospital in twenty minutes. I'll speak to the doctors and to Dad if he's able, then call you both with what I learn. Please keep your phones on, and let's decide together before I sign anything.

I'll go and sign whatever the doctor says is best. There's no time to discuss it, thinking about it now, I hadn't really thought it through, though I'm open to changing my mind — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.

I don't want to be the one to decide. Someone else will have to do it, I mean, I wasn't considering every angle, so feel free to push back — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet, and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
quests.hint: In a family emergency, take on the practical role, gather facts and keep everyone informed before big decisions.
quests.explanation: You are geographically the best placed, so acting as the eyes and ears is right, but decisions should be shared. Signing alone or refusing responsibility both fail the family.
consequencePreviews: You take responsibility for the practical step, gather facts and keep everyone in the decision.
As a result, deciding alone removes your siblings and may not reflect your father's wishes.
Here, withdrawing leaves the family without the person who is in a position to act.

quests.persona: a team leader, a new hire and a crisis
quests.scene: Your server goes down an hour before a major client demo. The new hire, who only started last week, thinks she knows the cause but is nervous about speaking. The senior engineer is unreachable.
options: We need someone experienced to handle this. Let's keep trying to reach the senior engineer.
Let's hear it, we've got nothing to lose. Tell me what you think and how sure you are. If it's low-risk to try, we'll test it in the staging copy first, and I'll take responsibility for the call.
Just go ahead and fix it however you think best. I trust you completely.
quests.hint: During an emergency, welcome input regardless of seniority, gauge how confident the person is, try it out in a low-risk way first, and own the outcome yourself.
quests.explanation: Time is short, so use every resource but limit risk with a staging test. Accountability protects the new hire. Insisting on seniority wastes time, and blind delegation is reckless.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, dismissing the new hire wastes valuable time and a potentially right answer.
As a result, you invite her idea, ask for confidence level, manage risk with a safe test and take accountability.
Here, handing over unchecked control in a crisis puts both of you at risk.
